clue.text: Vin rosé in the Bible?

parts.note: Surface reading: a pink wine turning up somewhere in scripture, perhaps at Cana.
Setter's reading: these seven letters are the word for a translation of a text, with its letters rearranged; the answer describes the clue.

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether rosé wine gets a mention in scripture.
explanation.walkthrough: This is a reverse anagram: the answer, read as an instruction, would turn VERSION into VIN ROSE. The Revised Version is the 1880s English Bible translation, so the phrase also names a Bible.
explanation.definitionFit: The Revised Version is a Victorian English translation of scripture, one of several named editions of the Christian holy book.

clue.text: Speak disparagingly of Danish outfit's almost burning dish

indicators.note: something almost complete stops just short, so the burning word loses its final letter

parts.note: to roast someone is to mock them harshly
FLAMBÉ, set alight, missing its last letter

explanation.surface: A critic sneers at a Danish company's dish that has nearly caught fire.
explanation.walkthrough: The word breaks of the answer fall nowhere near the clue's pieces, which is what hides it. 'Outfit' means a company here, not clothing; the toy firm is Danish.
explanation.definitionFit: A roasted joint from a young sheep's hind limb is a classic Sunday main course.

clue.text: State 'Former president's a bum!'

explanation.surface: Someone declares that an ex-president is a worthless layabout.
explanation.walkthrough: 'State' looks like a verb introducing the quotation; it is a US state, abbreviated. 'Bum' is the American sense, a tramp.
explanation.definitionFit: In American usage a bum is a homeless drifter with no fixed abode or work.

clue.text: Romanians deployed to enclave

indicators.note: troops deployed are spread out into new positions, so the nationality's letters take new places

explanation.surface: Romanian troops are sent into a small territory.
explanation.walkthrough: The nationality and the answer are both proper names from Europe, which helps the misdirection: the Romanians look like the subject, not the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: San Marino is a tiny republic wholly surrounded by Italian territory, which makes it a textbook enclave.

clue.text: Issue when beating up the guard

indicators.note: a phrase that is beaten up is knocked about and left in disorder, so its letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: A problem arises when a prison guard is assaulted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Issue' reads as a problem; here it is the old legal word for offspring.
explanation.definitionFit: Issue means children or descendants, especially in wills, and a female child is one such descendant.

clue.text: Railway station in Texas city announced by Cockney

indicators.note: something announced is spoken, and a Cockney speaker drops the opening H of the city

parts.note: Houston said with the H dropped

explanation.surface: A London station name is heard in a Texan city, spoken with a Cockney accent.
explanation.walkthrough: A Cockney is a working-class Londoner whose accent drops initial H, so Houston loses its first sound. Euston is a main-line terminus in London.
explanation.definitionFit: Euston is a major London rail terminus serving routes to the Midlands and north-west.

clue.text: Mountain covered by pianist from the East

indicators.note: the east is the right-hand side of a map, so starting there means reading right to left
what is covered by a word lies underneath it, so the mountain sits inside the musician

parts.note: the letters inside the musician's title, second to sixth

explanation.surface: A mountain is played over by a pianist from the Orient.
explanation.walkthrough: In an across-style reading the East is the right-hand end, so 'from the East' says read right to left; it looks like a description of the pianist's origin.
explanation.definitionFit: Mount Sinai is the peak in Egypt where Moses received the Ten Commandments.

clue.text: Sr., probably?

parts.note: Surface reading: a guess that this abbreviation stands for Senior.
Setter's reading: S and R are the first and third letters of the tail of the answer itself, so the answer split differently describes them.

explanation.surface: Someone guesses what the abbreviation after a name might mean.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as ODD SARE, the answer says: the odd letters of SARE, which are S and R. The question mark flags this self-referential trick.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom introduces a likely outcome, meaning it is more probable than not.

clue.text: Greek pentathletes injured, but perform bravely

indicators.note: injured athletes are damaged and out of shape, so their letters are reshaped

explanation.surface: Hurt Greek athletes carry on competing with courage.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue reads as a sports report, and 'Greek' belongs naturally to the ancient Olympics; only its abbreviation is used, with the rest of the fodder rearranged after it.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means tackling a difficult or painful task boldly, as seizing a stinging plant firmly stops it hurting.

clue.text: Oscar-winning movie fans kidnap a group of sailors

indicators.note: to kidnap is to seize and hold someone, so the fans hold the single letter inside them

explanation.surface: Film fans abduct a band of seamen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Oscar' tempts a solver toward the NATO alphabet letter O; here it is the Academy Award.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth Jason's crew who sailed the Argo in search of the Golden Fleece were known by this name.

clue.text: Rainstorm floods top of dance floor

indicators.note: water that floods a place surrounds it completely, so the jumbled weather letters go round the dance's letter
a storm whips things about, so the weather word's letters are thrown into a new order

parts.note: only the first four letters are fodder; the rest of the word is the anagram signal

indicators.note: the top of a word in an across clue is its first letter, so only the start of the dance is kept

parts.note: the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: A downpour pours in over the dance floor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rainstorm' is one word in the surface but splits into fodder and indicator. 'Floor' looks like part of 'dance floor'; it is the definition, meaning the lowest point.
explanation.definitionFit: A nadir is the lowest point of anything, a bottom level below which things cannot sink.

clue.text: Militia raid captures crown

indicators.note: the two words capture the answer, holding it prisoner across their join

parts.note: across the join of the two words

explanation.surface: Armed irregulars storm a place and seize a royal crown.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition sits at the end and the letters run across the word break, a standard hiding place.
explanation.definitionFit: A tiara is a jewelled ornamental headband, a type of small crown worn by royalty or brides.

clue.text: Hulk's smuggling crude oil for rough gang

indicators.note: a smuggler hides goods inside something, so the wrestler's name carries the oil within it

parts.note: Hulk Hogan, the American wrestler, with the possessive S

indicators.note: crude oil is unrefined and unprocessed, so its letters are not in finished order

explanation.surface: A ship's hulk is used to smuggle unrefined oil for a criminal gang.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hulk' reads as an old ship; it is a first name, and the surname of the wrestler Hulk Hogan is what goes around the oil.
explanation.definitionFit: Hooligans are violent, rowdy young troublemakers, often acting in groups.

clue.text: In dire need, sex is called for

indicators.note: the slang for sex is placed in the scrambled word, sitting inside it
a dire state is a terrible mess, so the following word's letters are in a mess

parts.note: slang for sex or sexual partners

explanation.surface: In desperate circumstances, sex is what's needed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In dire need' reads as one phrase; 'In' puts the slang word inside, and 'dire' scrambles 'need'.
explanation.definitionFit: If something entails an action it necessarily involves or requires it.

clue.text: Legal protection, plain as day

definitions.meaning: the exclusive right granted to an inventor

explanation.walkthrough: The noun protects an invention; the adjective means obvious, as in 'patent nonsense'.
explanation.definitionFit: An inventor's exclusive right is a legal safeguard; as an adjective the word means evident or unmistakable.

clue.text: Toothless bunch jury-rigged snare, snagging boob

indicators.note: a snare that snags something catches and holds it, so the rebuilt trap closes round the slang for a breast
something jury-rigged is cobbled together makeshift, so the trap's letters are rebuilt in a new order

parts.note: slang for a breast, and a nipple

explanation.surface: A gang of hapless people rig up a trap and it catches a blunder.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Toothless' reads as ineffective; it is literal, since these animals have no teeth. 'Boob' looks like a mistake but is the body part.
explanation.definitionFit: Anteaters are edentate mammals that lap insects with long tongues and have no teeth at all.

clue.text: Head wound where oceans meet

parts.note: to gore with horns, used as a verb

explanation.surface: A head injury is sustained at the meeting point of two seas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Head wound' reads as one injury; split, each word gives half. 'Wound' here is the past-tense-looking verb of injuring, not winding.
explanation.definitionFit: The southern tip of South America is where the Atlantic and Pacific waters come together.

clue.text: Cat that's spotted in the midst of grocery parcel

indicators.note: the midst of a word is its centre, so only the middle letters of the shop word are taken

parts.note: the three central letters of the shop word
a parcel of land or an auction lot

explanation.surface: A cat is seen among the groceries in a package.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spotted' reads as seen, making 'in the midst of' sound like where the cat was; it is the coat pattern, part of the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The ocelot is a wild American feline with a coat marked by dark rosettes and blotches.

clue.text: Gray's one with criminal ties around portion of Turkey

indicators.note: the jumbled ties are wrapped around the piece of the bird, enclosing it
criminal ties are crooked, bent out of true, so their letters are rearranged

parts.note: a leg is a joint of roast turkey

explanation.surface: Someone called Gray has shady links around part of the country Turkey.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital T makes Turkey the country; it is the bird. Thomas Gray wrote the 'Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard'.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas Gray is best known for a mournful poem of lament, making him a writer of that genre.

clue.text: Ill-treated ailments in uncaring workplace

indicators.note: ill-treated things are mishandled and knocked about, so the ailments are rearranged

explanation.surface: Sickness goes untreated in a callous place of employment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ill-treated' fits the medical surface of 'ailments' perfectly, which hides its job as the rearranging instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: Back to the salt mines is an idiom for returning to drudgery; the phrase stands for any grim job.

clue.text: Beer, I agree, is hoisted at beach

indicators.note: in a down entry, hoisting lifts something upward, so the word for agreement is read from bottom to top

parts.note: said to endorse a statement, as in amen to that

explanation.surface: Someone raises a beer at the seaside and says they agree.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue, 'hoisted' means read upward, so the word for agreement goes in back to front after the beer.
explanation.definitionFit: Ipanema is the famous stretch of sand in Rio de Janeiro, celebrated in the bossa nova song.

clue.text: Bowman's Spanish abode on the outskirts of Las Palmas

indicators.note: the outskirts of a town are its edges, so only the outer letters of the place name are used

parts.note: the first and last letters of the place name

explanation.surface: An archer owns a Spanish house on the edge of Las Palmas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bowman' suggests an archer; it is a cellist, who plays with a bow. Pablo Casals was the great Catalan cellist.
explanation.definitionFit: Pablo Casals was a celebrated Spanish cellist, and a string player draws music with a bow.

clue.text: Can't sleep in bunk at a sometimes raucous affair

parts.note: a gathering after a death, famously lively in Ireland

explanation.surface: Someone is kept up at night in their bunk bed at a noisy party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bunk' reads as a bed, fitting the sleepless surface; it is nonsense. A wake is a vigil or gathering for the dead that can turn boisterous.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who stays in bed unable to drop off is described with this phrase of wakefulness.

clue.text: Active ingredient at the heart of printer's ink colour

indicators.note: the heart is the core, so only the core survives and the first and last letters of the colour go

parts.note: the purplish-red of CMYK printing, with its outer letters removed

explanation.surface: The key chemical inside a printer's coloured ink.
explanation.walkthrough: The colour is magenta, the M of the CMYK inks used in colour printing; its middle five letters are kept.
explanation.definitionFit: A chemical substance that produces an effect, such as a cleaning or bleaching compound, is called by this name.

clue.text: A stride without delay

explanation.surface: A single long step taken in a hurry.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay is almost a straight synonym split in two, so the only step is seeing where the definition starts.
explanation.definitionFit: Apace is a literary adverb meaning swiftly or quickly, at a rapid speed.

clue.text: Audio puzzle — or what it may consist of

indicators.note: an audio puzzle is one you hear, so the word for puzzle is taken as it sounds

parts.note: a labyrinth is a puzzle to walk through

explanation.surface: A sound-based puzzle, and what that puzzle might be made up of.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It' refers back to the puzzle: farms cut maize mazes into cornfields as attractions, so the maze may consist of the crop.
explanation.definitionFit: Corn crops are planted tall and cut into paths to make a walk-through labyrinth.

clue.text: Reconciliation for Democrat, one mentally not all there

indicators.note: if the words are not all there, only a stretch of them is present, running across their joins

parts.note: runs from the end of the party word through to the start of the adverb

explanation.surface: A reconciliation is sought for a politician said to be mentally unstable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not all there' reads as an insult about the Democrat; it says only part of the words is used.
explanation.definitionFit: Making amends for wrongdoing restores harmony, and in theology the word means reconciling people with God.

clue.text: Argues in bad taste with boy, then strangely ceases

indicators.note: bad taste has gone off and spoiled, so the flavour word's letters are spoiled into a new order
something done strangely is done oddly and out of the usual order, so the final word is rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone quarrels offensively with a boy, then oddly stops.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In bad taste' reads as one phrase about rudeness; 'in' only joins the definition, and 'bad' rearranges the next word. Two separate anagrams sit either side of the boy.
explanation.definitionFit: To present your argument formally is to put forward reasons, as a lawyer does in court.
